definition: Articulatory phonology is a linguistic theory originally proposed in 1986 by Catherine Browman of Haskins Laboratories and Louis Goldstein of University of Southern California and Haskins.
details: The theory identifies theoretical discrepancies between phonetics and phonology and aims to unify the two by treating them as low- and high-dimensional descriptions of a single system. Unification can be achieved by incorporating into a single model the idea that the physical system (identified with phonetics) constrains the underlying abstract system (identified with phonology), making the units of control at the abstract planning level the same as those at the physical level. The plan of an utterance is formatted as a gestural score, which provides the input to a physically based model of speech production – the task dynamic model of Elliot Saltzman. The gestural score graphs locations within the vocal tract where constriction can occur, indicating the planned or target degree of constriction. A computational model of speech production developed at Haskins Laboratories combines articulatory phonology, task dynamics, and the Haskins articulatory synthesis system developed by Philip Rubin and colleagues.

explainer.lead: Articulatory phonology treats the abstract structure of speech and the physical movements that produce it as two views of one system. It matters because it offers a way to connect an utterance plan directly to a computational model of speech production.

tiers.eli5: Think of speech as a plan for moving parts of your mouth and throat, rather than as two separate subjects: one about ideas and one about movements. The plan works like a musical score, showing where and how much to narrow the pathway that air travels through. That score can then guide a computer model that produces speech.
tiers.practitioner: In a computational implementation, represent the utterance plan as a gestural score containing vocal-tract constriction locations and target constriction degrees, then feed it to Elliot Saltzman's task-dynamic model of speech production. The Haskins Laboratories model combines this approach with its articulatory synthesis system; a key pitfall is treating the gestural score as synthesized speech rather than as the plan supplied to the production model.
tiers.paperLevel: Proposed in 1986 by Catherine Browman of Haskins Laboratories and Louis Goldstein of the University of Southern California and Haskins, articulatory phonology defines phonetics and phonology as low- and high-dimensional descriptions of a single system. Its pipeline can be summarized as utterance plan -> gestural score G, specifying constriction locations and target degrees -> task-dynamic model -> physically based speech production. Physical constraints act on the abstract system so that the units of control at the planning and physical levels are the same.

explainer.example: For a particular utterance, its gestural score lists the relevant vocal-tract constriction locations and assigns each a planned target degree. That completed score becomes the input to the task-dynamic production model; in the Haskins computational implementation, articulatory phonology and task dynamics are combined with articulatory synthesis.

usedIn.name: Haskins computational speech-production model
usedIn.detail: Combines articulatory phonology, task dynamics, and the Haskins articulatory synthesis system.

usedIn.name: Task-dynamic speech modeling
usedIn.detail: Uses a gestural score as input to Elliot Saltzman's physically based model of speech production.

usedIn.name: Phonetics and phonology
usedIn.detail: Provides a common account of physical speech behavior and abstract phonological planning.

explainer.intuition: Instead of explaining physical speech and abstract sound structure with separate kinds of units, use the same units of control at both levels. The physical system constrains the abstract one, allowing phonetics and phonology to describe different dimensions of the same system.
howItWorks: Begin with the plan for an utterance.
Format that plan as a gestural score.
In the score, mark vocal-tract locations where constriction can occur and the planned or target degree of constriction.
Supply the score to Elliot Saltzman's task-dynamic model, which provides a physically based account of speech production.
explainer.whyItMatters: The theory addresses discrepancies between phonetics and phonology by placing them within one model rather than treating them as disconnected accounts. It also gives computational speech production an explicit, structured input: the gestural score.
misconceptions: It does not treat phonetics and phonology as independent systems; they are low- and high-dimensional descriptions of one system.
A gestural score is not the speech output itself; it is the utterance plan supplied to a production model.
The abstract planning units are not separate from physical control units; the theory makes them the same.
